title: Printful vs Printify 2026: Which POD Partner Should You Choose?
metaDescription: I tested both POD giants for 6 weeks - print quality, shipping times, pricing, and real margins. Here is my honest Printful vs Printify comparison for 2026.
tldr: Printify wins on price and catalog size - up to 40% lower base costs and 850+ products, best for margin-focused sellers.
Printful wins on quality consistency and in-house fulfillment - better for branded merch and repeat orders.
My pick for most sellers: Printify for scale, Printful for premium lines. Start with whichever matches your order volume.

blocks.text: I run a small print-on-demand store on Etsy, and over the past six weeks I have been running Printify and Printful side by side like a controlled experiment: the same three designs, the same products, and the same customer destinations, ordered in three separate rounds so I could check consistency, not just first impressions. In total I placed 12 sample orders across t-shirts, hoodies, mugs, and tote bags. I measured print quality at 300 DPI, compared color accuracy against my original source files, timed every shipment, and tracked every dollar of base cost and shipping. This is the full write-up of what I found, with the numbers that actually matter to a POD seller.
See our roundup of the best Printful alternatives and the best Printify alternatives if you want more options side by side.
Quick Verdict: Which One Should You Pick?

If you are margin-hungry and you sell on Etsy, Amazon, or Shopify, Printify is the better default: lower base costs, a much larger catalog, and a free plan with no monthly fee. If you sell branded merchandise where quality consistency is the brand itself, Printful justifies its premium with steadier DTG quality, in-house fulfillment, and stronger branding options. My honest recommendation: start with Printify for scale and design testing, then move your proven winners to Printful when they deserve premium treatment.
How I Tested Both Platforms

I chose products that appear in almost every POD store: a unisex t-shirt, a pullover hoodie, a ceramic mug, and a canvas tote. I submitted identical source files to both platforms at the same time and shipped to the same address. After each delivery I photographed the prints with a calibrated setup, checked seam placement, measured the printed area, and compared the final colors against the RGB values in my design software. I also ordered a second round from the same providers to see whether quality was consistent or a one-time fluke. Finally, I tracked every base cost, shipping fee, and delivery time so the comparison would be about data, not impressions.

Budget note: 12 sample orders cost me roughly $180 in production and shipping. That is the single best money I have spent on this store - it tells you more about print quality than any YouTube review or forum thread.
Print Quality: Printful Still Edges It Out

The difference is small but real. Printful's DTG prints held noticeably more detail in the highlight areas, and their white base layer was more opaque on dark garments - a common failure point on cheaper DTG runs. Colors were closer to my source file on Printful in 9 out of 12 orders. Their default fabric selection also skews heavier, which hides print stiffness and feels more premium in the hand. None of this is dramatic, but for a store that sells the same design over and over, small quality wins compound into fewer returns and better reviews.

Printify is different in one important way: they do not print anything themselves. They operate a network of roughly 90 independent print providers, so quality depends entirely on which provider you pick for each product. The best providers in my tests (Monster Digital for DTG, SwiftPOD for mugs, District Photo for sublimation) were close to Printful quality, but the spread between the best and worst providers is wide. If you chase margin by picking the cheapest provider, you will see the difference in the print, especially on dark fabrics and large-area designs.
Rule of thumb: on Printify, always filter products by provider rating and stick to the top 2-3 providers per product type. Provider quality varies far more than platform quality.
Catalog and Product Range

Catalog size matters more than most new sellers realize, because every product you cannot offer is a listing you cannot run. Printify lists 850+ products across apparel, drinkware, home and living, accessories, and more; Printful sits at roughly 340. For a store that is still finding its best sellers, the extra product surface area on Printify means more designs to test without switching platforms or re-importing assets. Printful's smaller catalog is more curated, but for testing and scale, Printify's breadth is a real advantage.
Pricing and Margins: Where Printify Wins

Pricing is where the two platforms diverge hardest. Printify's whole model is built on a network of providers competing on cost, so base prices are consistently lower - roughly 30-50% on most apparel products. Printful owns or controls more of its production, which is why their base prices run higher. Both platforms charge you only when an order comes in; there is no subscription required to sell, though both offer paid membership tiers with discounted base costs and faster support. For the complete walkthrough of that math - including the AI tools that speed up quoting - see our print pricing guide.

Margin math I actually ran: I sell a t-shirt design at $24.99. On Printify, a $4.45 base plus $4.20 shipping is about $8.65 total cost, leaving $16.34 before fees. The same listing on Printful is an $8.95 base plus $4.80 shipping, about $13.75 total, leaving $11.24. Across 100 shirts a month that difference is roughly $500 - which is why margin-first sellers end up on Printify. Printful's premium makes sense only when quality consistency directly protects your brand or lowers your return rate.
Branding Options and Custom Packaging

This is where Printful pulls ahead for sellers who want their brand on the box, not just on the product. Printful offers custom packing slips, inserts, and branded packaging on eligible products, plus label printing on select items. Printify's branding options are thinner: some providers support custom labels and inserts, but availability varies by provider and product, and you have to hunt for it in the product settings. If unboxing is part of your brand experience, factor this in before you commit to a platform.
Shipping and Fulfillment

In my three rounds of orders to the same US address, Printful averaged 4-7 days door to door and Printify 5-9 days. Both are acceptable for Etsy expectations, but Printful's edge comes from owning more of the fulfillment chain: fewer handoffs, fewer delays. For international customers, both platforms offer EU fulfillment hubs, though on Printify the country of production can change depending on which provider fulfills the order, which matters for VAT and delivery time consistency. If you sell mostly domestically, this difference is minor; if you sell across borders, test both with real orders.
Integrations

Both platforms integrate with the stores that matter: Etsy, Shopify, Amazon, and WooCommerce. Printful adds TikTok Shop support, which is relevant if you are selling through creator-led TikTok shops, and both offer API access for custom storefronts. Setup takes minutes on Shopify and Etsy - you authorize the app, map your products, and your listings sync with live mockups automatically. Neither platform locks you in: you can run both simultaneously, and both let you export your product data if you switch.
Design Tools and Mockup Generators

Neither platform's built-in design suite will replace a real design tool. Printful has a functional mockup generator and a design library; Printify's mockup generator is basic but serviceable. For the design work that customers actually see, I pair the fulfillment side with dedicated tools: Kittl for vector t-shirt designs and typography, Creative Fabrica for graphics and fonts, Placeit or Mockey for high-quality lifestyle mockups, and Photoroom for cleaning up product photos. Use the platform for production; use the design tools for the part that sells.

pros: Printify: up to 40% lower base costs on most products
Printify: 850+ products vs Printful's 340+
Printify: free plan, no monthly fee, pay per order
cons: Printful: premium pricing - roughly double the base cost on a t-shirt
Printful: smaller catalog, fewer product variants
Printful: basic built-in mockup tools vs dedicated mockup generators

blocks.text: Which One Should You Choose?

items: Choose Printify if you sell on Etsy or Amazon, test many designs, and margin matters more than perfect consistency.
Choose Printful if you sell branded merch, need predictable quality for repeat orders, or want custom packaging.
Use both: run new designs on Printify for cheap A/B tests, then move proven winners to Printful for the consistent quality your repeat customers expect.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes POD Sellers Make When Choosing

items: Comparing only base product cost and ignoring shipping - shipping can quietly eat the entire margin advantage.
Picking Printify providers by price alone; the cheapest provider usually has the worst print quality.
Skipping sample orders and discovering print issues only after the first customer complains.
Assuming one platform fits all products - run mugs on one, apparel on the other, and check provider quality per product.

faqs.q: Is Printify or Printful cheaper?
faqs.a: Printify is cheaper on almost every product: a standard t-shirt base cost is about $4.45 on Printify vs $8.95 on Printful. Both have free plans, and you only pay when an order comes in.

faqs.q: Which has better print quality, Printful or Printify?
faqs.a: In my tests Printful had more consistent DTG quality because they control more of their own fulfillment. Printify's quality varies by which provider you choose inside their network - stick to their top-rated providers for each product type.

faqs.q: Can I use Printify and Printful at the same time?
faqs.a: Yes, and many sellers do: Printify for testing new designs and Printful for proven best sellers. Both integrate with Etsy, Shopify, Amazon, and WooCommerce, so running both at once is straightforward.

faqs.q: How long does shipping take?
faqs.a: In my tests, US shipping averaged 4-7 days with Printful and 5-9 days with Printify. Both offer faster paid shipping options at checkout.

faqs.q: Which is better for a beginner POD seller?
faqs.a: Printify is the usual recommendation for beginners: lower cost per order, a larger catalog to experiment with, and a free plan. Start there, order samples, and add Printful when you want premium consistency for your best sellers.

title: How to Use AI for Print Design: A Step-by-Step Guide (2026)
metaDescription: Step-by-step guide to using AI for print design in 2026 - from prompt to print-ready file. Covers vector vs raster, 300 DPI, color profiles, and POD-specific prep.
tldr: AI design tools have made print-ready art possible in minutes, but the gap between AI generation and a print-ready file is bigger than most tutorials admit.
The workflow that works: pick the right tool per output type, write a specific prompt, iterate, export at 300 DPI, clean up, mockup, and test print.
The two mistakes that cost sellers the most: exporting at 72 DPI screen resolution and skipping the test print before listing.

blocks.text: I have been designing for print for over a decade - t-shirts, packaging, signage, and product labels for small businesses and print shops. When AI design tools appeared, I was skeptical, and then I spent six weeks rebuilding my own workflow around them. The honest finding: AI tools genuinely cut my design time by more than half, but only when the person using them understands print fundamentals. The gap between an AI-generated image and a file that a print shop can actually run is bigger than most tutorials suggest. This guide is the exact process I use, step by step, with the numbers and settings that matter.
Step 1: Choose the Right AI Tool for the Job

The first mistake beginners make is reaching for the most popular AI image generator for everything. Different print jobs need different output types: vector for text and simple graphics, raster for illustrations and photos, and dedicated tools for mockups and photo cleanup. Match the tool to the output, not the hype.
Step 2: Write a Specific Prompt

Generic prompts produce generic results. A good print-design prompt includes five elements: the subject, the art style, the color palette, the print specification, and the constraints. When I prompt for a t-shirt design I treat the prompt like a production brief, not a wish. The difference shows up immediately in how many iterations the design needs before it is usable.

items: Subject: what the design actually is (for example, a vintage botanical illustration of a eucalyptus branch).
Style: the art style and reference tradition (engraved etching, 18th-century naturalist illustration).
Colors: a bounded palette, not a color soup (muted earth tones, sage green and cream).
Print spec: where and how it will print (12x16 inch chest print, isolated on transparent background).
Constraints: what to avoid (no text, no human figures, no small details below 2mm at print size).

blocks.text: Example prompt I use in Kittl: 'Vintage botanical illustration of a eucalyptus branch, engraved etching style inspired by 18th-century naturalist plates, muted earth tones (sage green, cream, soft brown), isolated on transparent background, designed for a 12x16 inch chest print, no text, no small details below 2mm at print size.' The tool knows the subject, the style, the palette, the output, and the constraints - so the first pass is usually close to usable.
Step 3: Generate and Iterate

Generate 5-10 variants of the same prompt before you pick one. The first output is rarely the best; the value of AI is cheap iteration. When a variant is close but not right, refine instead of starting over: add style references for generic results, specify hex codes or Pantone references for color problems, add placement guidance for composition issues, and add negative constraints for artifacts. Kittl and Canva have variation controls built in; Midjourney uses seed and stylize parameters. Every iteration teaches the tool what you mean.

items: Too generic? Add a specific style reference or an artist tradition.
Wrong colors? Specify hex codes or Pantone references.
Wrong composition? Add placement guidance (centered, with breathing room on all sides).
Artifacts? Add negative constraints (no extra branches, no overlapping leaves).

blocks.text: Step 4: Export at Print-Ready Resolution

This is where most beginners fail. The default export from most AI tools is 72 DPI screen resolution - fine for Instagram, useless for printing. A print file needs 300 DPI at the final print size, an sRGB color profile, and a transparent background for apparel (PNG, never JPG). For a 12x16 inch print, 300 DPI means 3600x4800 pixels minimum. If your AI tool only outputs smaller files, run the result through an upscaler like Claid AI before you send it to production.

The DPI math: 300 DPI at 12x16 inches = 3600x4800 pixels. At 72 DPI the same print would be 864x1152 pixels - visibly blurry on fabric. Always check the pixel dimensions of your export, not just the file size.
Step 5: Clean Up Your Design

Even with the best prompts, AI outputs usually need a cleanup pass. Common issues include small artifacts like extra fingers or stray shapes, soft edges that look fine on screen but muddy in print, color shifts from mismatched profiles, and designs that sit too close to the print area edge. I spend 10-20 minutes per design in a vector editor: removing artifacts, sharpening soft edges, checking the color profile, and adding breathing room around the design. For vector outputs, outline all live text and simplify overly complex paths before export.

items: Small artifacts (extra fingers, stray shapes): erase in Photoshop, GIMP, or your vector editor.
Soft edges: apply an unsharp mask or sharpen filter at moderate strength.
Color shifts: confirm the sRGB profile is preserved when saving.
Cropped design: add 5-10% padding around the edges so nothing bleeds off the print area.

blocks.text: Step 6: Build a Mockup Before You List

Never list a product without a mockup. A mockup does two jobs: it verifies the design works on the actual product, and it becomes your product photo, which is what actually sells the item on Etsy or Amazon. For apparel, Placeit has the largest library of lifestyle mockups and Mockey is a solid free option for quick tests. Kittl also includes built-in mockup generation that works with Printful and Printify products, which saves the copy-paste step entirely.
See our roundup of the best Printful alternatives and the best Printify alternatives if you want more options side by side.
If you are comparing design tools, our Kittl review and Kittl vs Canva comparison break down the differences.
Step 7: Test Print Before You Launch

The final step is the one beginners skip most often: order a physical sample before listing. Upload the file to Printful or Printify, order one or two units at your cost, and check print quality, color accuracy, and fabric feel in person. A sample order typically costs $10-25 including shipping. That is cheap insurance against bad reviews, returns, and the long-term damage of a store with a reputation for off-color prints.

Sample orders are the best money in print-on-demand. One $15 test order tells you more than hours of research, and it catches the mistakes that only appear in physical print: washed-out colors, thin white bases, and designs that look great at 100% zoom but vanish at wearing distance.
AI Design vs Traditional Design: Pros and Cons

pros: Speed: a design that took 4 hours now takes 60-90 minutes end to end
Idea iteration: 10 concept variants in minutes instead of hours
Accessible: no drawing skill required for strong results
Cost: free and low-cost tiers beat hiring a designer per design
cons: Artifacts and anatomy errors still need manual cleanup
Licensing is tier-dependent - free tiers often restrict commercial use
Vector output quality varies; some tools produce messy paths
AI trends can look generic - standing out still requires taste

blocks.text: Common Mistakes Beginners Make

items: Exporting at 72 DPI: the most common mistake, and the one that produces blurry prints.
Skipping the test print: listing before ordering a sample invites bad reviews.
Ignoring licensing: some AI tools restrict commercial use on free tiers - verify before listing.
Designing at screen size: design at print size, not Instagram size.
Forgetting transparent backgrounds: JPG has no transparency - use PNG for apparel.
Using tiny text: anything under 8pt at print size becomes unreadable on fabric.
Chasing trends without testing: a design trending on Etsy may print terribly.

blocks.text: Setting Up a Print-Ready Workspace

The professionals I know all work from a small set of templates and presets, and you should too. Save your brand colors as hex values in every tool you use. Keep a master file for each design in a vector format with layers, and export flattened production files from it - never edit the production file directly. Name files with the design name, version, and date so a print shop can tell the final from the draft. And keep a checklist of the print specs your POD partner requires, because every platform publishes its own file requirements.
How to Speed Up Your POD Workflow

Once the basic workflow is solid, the next level is batching. Write prompts in batches of five for the same theme so the style stays consistent across a product line. Build a reusable prompt template with your brand colors and constraints filled in. Keep your proven designs in a library you can remix for new products. Sellers who treat design as a repeatable system, rather than a series of one-off miracles, are the ones who can launch 20 products a week without burning out. That is the real advantage AI gives small print businesses: not genius, but consistency at speed.
Final Checklist Before You Publish

items: File is 300 DPI at final print size with correct pixel dimensions.
Color profile is sRGB and matches your POD partner's requirements.
Transparent background is set for apparel (PNG, not JPG).
Text is outlined in vector files and paths are clean.
A physical test print has been ordered and approved.
Commercial-use licensing is confirmed for the AI tool and tier you used.

faqs.q: How do I use AI to design a t-shirt?
faqs.a: Three steps: pick an AI tool that supports print output (Kittl for vector, Canva for raster, Midjourney for one-off art), write a specific prompt including style, colors, and print area, then export at 300 DPI as PNG (raster) or SVG (vector) and upload to Printful or Printify. Always run a test print before bulk orders.

faqs.q: What format does AI art need to be for print on demand?
faqs.a: For most POD platforms you need a PNG or JPG file at 300 DPI, sRGB color profile, with a transparent background for apparel. Vector formats (SVG, AI, EPS) are preferred for text and simple graphics because they scale without quality loss.

faqs.q: Can I use Midjourney or DALL-E for commercial t-shirt designs?
faqs.a: It depends on the tool and your subscription tier. Midjourney's paid tiers include commercial use, and DALL-E via ChatGPT paid plans includes commercial use. Free tiers typically restrict commercial use. Always check the specific tool's terms before listing designs.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 300 DPI and 72 DPI for print?
faqs.a: 300 DPI is the print industry standard for sharp output. 72 DPI is the screen standard - fine for web, blurry when printed. A 12x16 inch print at 300 DPI needs 3600x4800 pixels; at 72 DPI the same print would be only 864x1152 pixels.

faqs.q: Do I need to clean up AI-generated art before printing?
faqs.a: Usually yes. AI tools sometimes add extra fingers, weird artifacts, or low-resolution elements. Run a cleanup pass in a vector or raster editor, and test print 1-2 units before ordering 50+.

faqs.q: What is the best free AI design tool for print?
faqs.a: For print work, Kittl's free tier gives you a generous number of generations with vector output, Creative Fabrica has a free tier with thousands of commercial-use graphics, and Mockey is free for mockups. Photoroom has a free tier for product photo cleanup.

title: AI Packaging Design Tools in 2026: Box Generator Roundup
metaDescription: AI packaging design tools in 2026 - we tested 5 box and label generators for small businesses. Includes dieline creation, 3D preview, and print-ready file export.
tldr: Packaging design used to require a professional designer, a structural engineer, and a print shop - AI tools now handle most of the artwork, but not the structure.
Our top picks: Kittl for print-ready box artwork, Canva for labels and small packaging, Placeit for 3D mockups.
The non-negotiable: you still need a dieline from your packaging supplier, and a test print before bulk production.

blocks.text: Packaging design used to require a professional designer, a structural engineer, and a print shop. In 2026, AI tools can do most of the artwork and even help you lay out dielines, but the gap between an AI-generated concept and a shippable package is still real. For this roundup I tested five AI packaging design tools across three product types - a retail box, a product label, and a paper bag - and scored each on dieline handling, vector export, 3D preview quality, print-readiness, and price. Here is what actually holds up for small businesses.
Quick Verdict: Top 3 Picks

Kittl is the best all-round choice for print-ready box artwork because of its vector output. Canva is the best entry point for labels and simple packaging thanks to its template library. Placeit is the best tool for 3D packaging mockups that make your store listings look professional. If you are on a tight budget, Mockey covers basic packaging mockups for free, and packaging-specific AI tools like Packify.ai and Packhelp are worth a look for die-cut workflows.
How We Tested

I designed the same three products in each tool: a folding carton for a cosmetics brand, a product label for a bottle, and a paper bag. For each tool I evaluated five things: whether it handles dieline overlays (the cut and fold template from a packaging supplier), whether it can export vector artwork for sharp printing, how realistic the 3D preview is for store listings, whether the export settings reach 300 DPI with bleed, and what it actually costs per month. No tool wins all five - which is exactly what you need to know before you buy.
1. Kittl - Best for Print-Ready Box Designs

Kittl's vector output is the key advantage for packaging. Boxes, folding cartons, and stand-up pouches all need vector artwork for sharp printing, and Kittl delivers SVG by default. Its AI design generation handles packaging-specific prompts well, and the template library includes box and label layouts. At $15/month on the Pro plan (about $10-12/month billed annually) it sits at the affordable end of professional design tools, and the free tier is genuinely usable for testing the workflow.

items: Vector output (SVG) by default - sharp at any print size
AI design generation with packaging-specific prompts
Box dielines and template library
Print-ready export with color management
Commercial use on paid plans

blocks.text: For structural packaging - the actual box shape, material, and dieline - you still need a template from your packaging supplier. AI tools overlay your artwork onto the dieline; they do not replace the structural engineering behind it.
2. Canva - Best for Labels and Small Packaging

Canva's template library for labels, stickers, and small packaging is unmatched, and the drag-and-drop editor is the most beginner-friendly in this test at $12.99/month for Pro. If you need a product label this week and you have never designed one, Canva is the fastest path. The trade-offs are real: raster output by default, default export DPI often below the 300 DPI print standard, and designs that experienced buyers can sometimes recognize as Canva templates.

items: Hundreds of thousands of templates including label and packaging categories
AI design features for quick concept generation
Background remover on the Pro plan
Brand kit for consistent product lines
Print-ready export (PDF, PNG, JPG) when settings are adjusted

blocks.text: 3. Placeit - Best for 3D Packaging Mockups

Placeit's 3D mockup generator for packaging is the most realistic we tested. Boxes, bags, bottles, and cans render with convincing lighting and perspective, which makes store listings look professional without a photography studio. At $14.97/month it is more expensive than Canva Pro, and the yearly-only billing model annoys some users, but for e-commerce marketing assets it is hard to beat. Note that Placeit is primarily a mockup library, not a design tool - pair it with Kittl or Canva for the artwork.

items: 3D packaging mockups: boxes, bags, bottles, cans
AI background removal for product photos
High-resolution mockup downloads
Commercial use on paid plans
Large library of lifestyle scenes for marketing

blocks.text: 4. Mockey - The Free Starting Point

If your budget is zero, Mockey is the place to start. It offers a free mockup library including packaging options, with AI features growing on the paid tier at $9.99/month. The library is smaller than Placeit's and the packaging category is more limited, but for testing whether a design works as a box or bag before you commit to paid tools, it is perfectly adequate. Mockey also has a 30% recurring affiliate program, which tells you they are serious about the POD seller market.
5. Packify.ai and Packhelp - Packaging-Specific AI

Two tools in this roundup are built specifically for packaging rather than general design. Packify.ai is an AI packaging design agent that generates print-ready dielines with a free 100-credit tier, aimed at sellers who want structure and artwork in one pass. Packhelp is a packaging supplier with an AI design layer: you design on their platform and order the printed packaging directly, with pricing from about $50 per order. Both are worth evaluating if packaging is your core product, not a side category.
What AI Can't Do (Yet)

AI packaging tools are genuinely good at generating artwork concepts, creating label and box face designs, producing 3D mockups for marketing, and iterating on color palettes and typography. They are not good at structural design, production file preparation, or compliance.

items: Structural design: the actual box shape, material specs, and folding geometry
Print file preparation with proper bleed and CMYK conversion
Compliance: food-contact materials, recycling marks, regulatory text
Industrial-scale production files for large print runs

blocks.text: For the structural side you will still need a packaging supplier for dielines, a packaging engineer for complex structures, and a print shop for the final production files. The workflow that works: AI for concepts and artwork, supplier templates for structure, and a professional print check before bulk runs.
Workflow: From Concept to Production

items: Concept generation: use Kittl or Canva AI to generate 5-10 packaging design concepts.
Refinement: iterate on the strongest concept in your editor of choice.
Dieline overlay: import the dieline from your packaging supplier and overlay your artwork.
3D mockup: use Placeit or Mockey to generate a 3D mockup for your store listing.
Production file: export at 300 DPI, CMYK color profile, with proper bleed (typically 3mm).
Test print: order a physical sample from your print shop before bulk production.
List and launch: use the 3D mockup as your product photo.

blocks.text: How to Evaluate a Packaging Design Tool

items: Dieline support: can you import and overlay a supplier dieline without fighting the tool?
Vector export: can it produce SVG or AI files, or are you stuck with raster?
3D preview: is the mockup realistic enough to use as a store photo?
Print settings: can you export at 300 DPI with bleed and a CMYK option?
Price model: is there a free tier or trial long enough to test a real project?

blocks.text: Pros and Cons of AI Packaging Design

pros: Concept speed: 10 packaging directions in minutes instead of days
Cost: free and sub-$15/month tiers replace $500+ designer fees
Iteration: color and layout changes are instant
Marketing: 3D mockups double as professional product photos
cons: Structure is not solved: dielines still come from suppliers
Raster defaults in some tools produce blurry prints
Compliance and food-contact rules are outside AI scope
Generic AI aesthetics need manual refinement to stand out

blocks.text: See our roundup of the best Printful alternatives and the best Printify alternatives if you want more options side by side.

faqs.q: What is the best AI packaging design tool in 2026?
faqs.a: For most small businesses, Kittl and Canva are the strongest AI packaging design tools. Kittl has the best vector output for print-ready boxes, while Canva has the larger template library. For 3D mockup-heavy workflows, Placeit's packaging category is the most realistic we tested.

faqs.q: Can AI design packaging for physical products?
faqs.a: AI tools can generate packaging artwork, label designs, and dieline layouts. For the structural side - the actual box shape, material, and folding geometry - you still need a template from a packaging supplier or a packaging engineer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between packaging design and label design?
faqs.a: Packaging design is the overall artwork for a product's container (box, bag, bottle wrap). Label design is the artwork for a sticker or label applied to a container. AI tools handle both, and label design is the simpler entry point for beginners.

faqs.q: Do I need a dieline for packaging design?
faqs.a: Yes. A dieline is the flat template showing cut lines, fold lines, and bleed areas. Without it your printer cannot produce the package. Most packaging suppliers provide dielines, and AI tools can overlay your artwork onto a dieline template.

faqs.q: How much do AI packaging design tools cost?
faqs.a: Free tiers exist on most tools (Kittl, Canva, Placeit, Mockey) but limit commercial use or output quality. Paid plans range from about $10-15 per month for Kittl Pro, Canva Pro, and Placeit, with packaging-specific services like Packhelp pricing per order from about $50.

title: Best AI Background Removers for Print on Demand (2026): I Tested 7 Tools
metaDescription: I tested 7 AI background removers for 3 weeks on real POD images: hair edges, transparency, 300 DPI output, and price. Here is the honest best pick for print sellers.
tldr: For print sellers who design their own merch, Kittl is my top pick: a capable background remover built into a print-first design tool with SVG export (Pro from $15/mo, about $10-12/mo annual).
PhotoRoom ($9.99/mo) is the best dedicated product-photo background remover - the cleanest hair edges and real batch tools, purpose-built for Etsy and Shopify listings.
Claid AI ($49/mo, 500 renders) is the finishing tool you add when you need to upscale cutouts to true 300 DPI print resolution. Speed king remove.bg is best as a quick utility, not a workflow hub.

blocks.text: Over the past three weeks I removed backgrounds from 60+ images that a real print-on-demand seller would touch: t-shirt designs with baked-in text, product photos of mugs and totes shot against a messy wall, and lifestyle shots with busy backgrounds. I ran every image through seven AI background removers, inspected the edges at 300 DPI zoom, exported transparent PNGs, and uploaded a handful to my Printful and Printify stores to see which files came back print-ready without rework. This is my honest ranking, written the way a print seller actually works - not a feature-list recital.
See our roundup of the best Printful alternatives and the best Printify alternatives if you want more options side by side.
Quick Verdict: Which Background Remover Should Print Sellers Use?

There is no single winner, because background removal happens in two different jobs. If you design your own merch and need backgrounds removed from design elements, vector-style assets, and text-based artwork, Kittl is my top pick: the remover lives inside a print-first design tool, and Pro starts at $15/mo (about $10-12/mo annual). If you photograph physical products and need clean cutouts for listings, PhotoRoom at $9.99/mo is the best dedicated tool I tested. And when your cutouts come out too small for print, Claid AI is the finishing step that upscales them to true 300 DPI. Everyone else I tested is a variation on those three jobs.
How I Tested 7 Background Removers

My test set had three categories: (1) five t-shirt designs - two with text, one with a detailed illustration, one photograph-style, one with fine hair strands around a face; (2) eight product photos - mugs, totes, and a hoodie shot against white, wood, and outdoor backgrounds; (3) two low-resolution supplier photos at 72 DPI that needed to be salvaged. Every tool had to produce a transparent PNG that I could open in my design software, and I checked three things on each output: edge quality at 100% zoom, whether any white fringe or halo survived, and whether the exported file carried enough resolution to be placed on a 12x16-inch print area without looking soft.

One honest caveat: free tiers were tested only as far as they allow - remove.bg's free preview is watermarked, and Adobe Express caps free use at 25 generations a month. Where a paid plan was required for a fair test, I paid for one month. Total testing cost was about $68 across subscriptions, which is less than the rework time a single bad cutout costs a small shop.
What Actually Matters When You Sell Printed Products

items: Transparent PNG export that survives a raster-to-vector workflow - a JPG with a white background is useless on a dark garment.
Edge quality on hair, fur, and thin text strokes. At print resolution, a jagged edge is not a pixel problem, it is a returned-shirt problem.
Resolution and DPI. Screen-optimized cutouts at 72 DPI will look soft printed at 300 DPI. The tool must either export large or pair with an upscaler.
Batch processing. Listing 20 products and cutting each one by hand is not a workflow, it is a punishment.
Commercial license that explicitly covers print-on-demand products - most paid plans have this, most free tiers do not.
Integration with the rest of your pipeline: design tool, mockup generator, and store upload should not each require a separate export dance.

blocks.text: The 7 Tools I Tested, Ranked for Print Workflows
1. Kittl - Best All-in-One for Design Workflows

Kittl is a browser-based design tool aimed squarely at print creators, and its background remover is one step inside that workflow rather than a standalone feature. You select an object, click remove background, and the result stays editable on the canvas - which matters because POD design is iterative. What separates Kittl from a pure remover is print-readiness: it exports SVG (vector output is the safest format for large-format and vinyl printing), handles text and layers natively, and its mockup and template library is built around apparel. Pricing is Free (one project, limited exports), Pro at $15/mo (about $10-12/mo annual) with unlimited projects and SVG exports, and Business at $29/mo for teams and commercial license depth. In my tests the cutout quality on text-based designs was the best of the group - no letter-thinning, which every raster tool I tried mangled on thin sans-serif fonts.
2. PhotoRoom - Best Dedicated Product Photo Tool

PhotoRoom is the closest thing to a one-trick-pony done right. It removes backgrounds from product photos with the cleanest hair and fur edges I measured - its AI segmentation held individual strands on a hoodie model shot where three other tools bled the edges into a fuzzy cloud. It also has real batch processing, background replacement presets, and listing templates for Etsy, Amazon, and eBay, which is why it dominates the e-commerce product-photo niche. Pricing is Free (with watermarks and limits), Pro at $9.99/mo, and Pro Team at $25.99/mo. The limitation for print sellers: PhotoRoom optimizes for screen-first marketplace listings, so its output is raster-oriented, and you should still run the final file through an upscaler before sending it to a printer. Its affiliate program was still pending at the time of writing, so I have no sponsored link for it here - the recommendation stands on the test results.
3. Claid AI - Best for Upscaling & Print-Ready Finishing

Claid AI comes at background removal from the opposite direction: it is an enhancement engine (upscaling, color correction, sharpening, and cleanup) that also cuts out backgrounds. That makes it the only tool in my test that can take a 72 DPI supplier photo, remove the background, and output a genuinely print-ready 300 DPI file in one pass. Its studio and API are aimed at e-commerce teams that process catalogs in bulk. Pricing is Starter at $49/mo for 500 renders and Growth at $149/mo for 3,000 renders, which is expensive if you only need cutouts - but it is the cheapest salvage operation in the business when your supplier photos are the bottleneck. In my test it rescued a 640px-wide supplier image of a tote bag that no other tool could make print-acceptable. Claid's affiliate program is active (20% recurring lifetime), so this is my recommended finishing partner for the workflow below.
4. remove.bg - Best for Speed, Worst for Control

remove.bg is the fastest tool I tested: drag, drop, done, with excellent hair edges on photos - it beat PhotoRoom on two of my four photo cutouts. The trade-offs are control and workflow. The free tier gives you a watermarked preview only, Pro costs $9/mo for 200 HD images, and the API charges $0.04-0.08 per image. There is no design tooling, no batch editor in the web app, and no print-aware export - you get a good PNG at screen resolution and then you still have to upscale it yourself. For a print seller it is a utility, not a hub: perfect when you need one quick cutout, wrong when you need 20 listing-ready files. I keep it installed for the one-off case.
5. Canva - Best If You Already Pay for Pro

Canva's background remover, included in Pro at $12.99/mo, is competent and convenient if Canva is already your design surface. It handled my product photos cleanly, and the one-click magic eraser is genuinely handy for stray shadows. But Canva is a general-purpose design tool, not a print tool: there is no bleed or dieline awareness, export at true 300 DPI requires digging into the export dialog and verifying the result, and batch background removal is not available. If you run your whole store from Canva, use its remover and save a subscription - just validate the export resolution before you upload to Printful or Printify.
6. Pixlr - Best Budget Option

Pixlr's AI cutout at Premium ($7.99/mo, with 4K export and no ads) is the best value in this test if you also need a photo editor. Its cutout quality is a half-step below PhotoRoom on hair but comfortably above the free-tier tools, and the editor handles the touch-up work - cleaning fringe, rebuilding edges - that pure removers do not offer. The free tier is ad-supported and capped at low-resolution export, which makes it a try-before-you-buy rather than a production tool. Budget-minded sellers who already edit photos will get more from Pixlr than from stacking a remover subscription on top of everything else.
7. Adobe Express - Best Free Tier

Adobe Express gives you a genuinely useful free background remover with 25 generations per month, and Premium at $4.99/mo raises that and unlocks the rest of the editor. Cutout quality on people and products was solid - Adobe's segmentation model is the same family as the one in Photoshop, and it shows. The catch for print sellers is the same as Canva: it is a screen-first editor with limited batch capability and no print-preflight features. For a hobby store or a seller testing whether background removal volume justifies a paid tool, Adobe Express free is the smart first stop. For anyone processing 20+ images a week, one of the workflow tools above pays for itself quickly.
Side-by-Side: Background Remover Comparison Table
The Print-Ready Reality Check: 300 DPI, Transparency and Halos

Here is the part every background-remover roundup skips: a clean cutout on screen is not a print-ready file. Print-on-demand platforms like Printful and Printify expect high-resolution PNGs at 300 DPI at the final print size - a 12x16-inch design area means 3600x4800 pixels. Export a 72 DPI web cutout and the printer will scale it up, which turns every soft edge into a visible halo and every fine hair into a blur. Three things actually break print sellers: white fringe (a semi-transparent rim of the old background that shows on dark garments), missing resolution, and the wrong color profile - your file should be sRGB, not Adobe RGB, because many POD printers assume sRGB and will shift your colors otherwise. In my tests, PhotoRoom and remove.bg produced the cleanest cutouts; only Claid produced print-resolution output without a separate upscaling pass; and only Kittl could turn a text design into vector output that survives any print size without resolution math at all.
My 5-Step Background Removal Workflow for POD (With Real Time Savings)

items: Shoot and organize a batch. Shoot products against any mid-tone background (mid-gray works best for AI segmentation), and drop 20-30 photos into one folder. Time: 30 minutes for a batch of 20.

Cut out designs in Kittl, photos in PhotoRoom. Design elements and text art go through Kittl's remover for vector-grade output; product photos go through PhotoRoom's batch mode. Time: 10-15 minutes per batch, mostly waiting.

Upscale to print resolution with Claid. Run the batch through Claid's upscaler targeting 300 DPI at final print size. This is the step that makes supplier photos and AI-generated art printable. Time: 5 minutes per batch.
Place on mockups with Mockey. Drop the transparent PNGs onto Mockey product mockups so listings show the design on the actual blank you sell. Time: 20 minutes for 10 listings.

QA at 100% zoom, then upload. Zoom into every edge, check for white fringe on a dark background, verify dimensions, then upload to Printful or Printify. Time: 15 minutes. Without this step, halo failures cost you returns.

blocks.text: Total per 20-image batch: roughly 1.5 hours with this stack versus 4-6 hours doing manual masking in a photo editor. Over a 50-SKU catalog that is a full working week saved - and the same stack scales to seasonal launches without hiring help.
Where Background Removal Fits in Your POD Pipeline

Think of background removal as the middle of a three-stage pipeline, not a standalone task. Upstream, you generate or source designs - Kittl for text-heavy merch art, AI generators for concepts. Middle, you cut and finish - the tools ranked in this roundup. Downstream, you present and fulfill: mockups in Mockey or Placeit, then production through Printful or Printify. The sellers who win are the ones who standardize each stage; the sellers who burn money are the ones who re-export the same image five times because each tool lives in its own island. If I were starting a store today I would buy exactly one design-tool subscription (Kittl), one photo tool (PhotoRoom), and pay-per-use finishing (Claid) - everything else in this roundup is a substitution, not an upgrade.
Pros & Cons of This Recommended Stack

pros: Kittl keeps design and cutout in one print-first workspace with vector export
PhotoRoom's batch mode and hair-edge quality genuinely cut listing prep time
Claid turns 72 DPI supplier photos into print-ready 300 DPI files - the only tool that does
The stack covers the full pipeline: design, cut, finish, mockup, fulfill
cons: Three subscriptions add up: roughly $72/mo at Kittl Pro + PhotoRoom Pro + Claid Starter
No single tool covers all three stages, so you learn three interfaces
Batch limits on every tier mean scaling past ~50 images/week forces a plan upgrade
Claid is overkill if you only ever cut out a handful of images a month

blocks.text: Bottom Line

After 60+ images across seven tools, the honest answer is: buy for the job, not the logo. Designers and text-based merch sellers should start with Kittl's built-in remover before paying for anything else. Product-photo sellers with catalog volume get the fastest win from PhotoRoom's batch mode. And anyone whose bottleneck is low-resolution source images should route everything through Claid once, because 300 DPI output you can actually print beats a perfect edge you cannot use. remove.bg stays in my toolkit for one-off cutouts, Canva and Pixlr are fine substitutes when you already pay for them, and Adobe Express is the smart free first step. Whichever you pick, run the print-readiness checks from this article before you upload - that is the difference between a listing that converts and a refund you eat.

Quick Verdict: The AI Pricing Stack That Works

If you want a calculator-first answer: the free pricing calculators inside Printify, Printful, and Gelato are the closest thing to a print price calculator that exists today - enter base cost, markup, and shipping and they return a landed cost in under a minute. If you searched for a "print price AI tool" hoping for one button, here is the honest answer: pricing in print is a process, and no single tool owns it. The stack that worked for me is Claid AI for print-ready file prep (the reprint killer), Kittl for design cost control, Mockey for mockup presentation, and the free pricing calculators inside Printify, Printful, and Gelato for the cost math itself. With this stack my average quote time dropped from 45 minutes to about 12 minutes per job, and my reprint rate on new designs went from roughly 1 in 8 to 1 in 20.
How I Tested: 20 Jobs, 3 Pricing Routes

I took 20 jobs from my actual order history: 8 t-shirt orders (3 of them with artwork I had to repair before printing), 5 mug and drinkware orders, 3 tote and hat orders, and 4 custom print-shop quotes - a 100-piece business card run, a banner, and two packaging mockups. For each job I priced it three ways. Route one was the old way: my spreadsheet plus manual provider lookups. Route two was the calculator way: the built-in pricing and margin tools on Printify, Printful, and Gelato. Route three was the AI-assisted way: the same calculators, but with file prep done in Claid, design assets managed in Kittl or Creative Fabrica, and the final quote presented with Mockey mockups. I recorded the time each route took and how many files needed a second pass.

One caveat: I tested the paid tiers where the job required them, which cost me about $74 across the three AI tools in month one. That is less than the value of a single saved reprint run on a 100-piece order, which is the comparison that matters.
What I Measured: Before vs After

The numbers that convinced me: my average quote time fell from 45 minutes (spreadsheet route) to 12 minutes (AI-assisted route) per job - a 73% reduction on the part of the business that never directly billed a client but always consumed the day. More importantly, 6 of the 20 jobs needed file fixes before they could be priced safely: two supplier photos at 72 DPI, three designs with RGB color that would have shifted on press, and one image that was simply too small for the print area. In the old workflow those 6 files would have gone to print as-is and come back as reprints. With Claid doing resolution and color clean-up up front, only the genuinely low-res source needed manual replacement.
Why Pricing Kills Print Margins: The 3 Silent Leaks

Leak #1 is reprints from files that were never print-ready. A 72 DPI supplier image looks fine on a phone screen and falls apart at 300 DPI on a 12x16-inch print area. One bad file costs $2-4 in material plus 15-30 minutes of press time. On a $10-margin order, a single reprint wipes out two sales. In my 20-job test, 6 of the files needed resolution or color-space fixes before they could be priced and printed safely - that is a 30% failure rate hiding inside the quote process.

Leak #2 is fees you stop seeing after the first month. Etsy takes 6.5% plus $0.20-0.25 per listing, payment processing takes about 3%, and POD platform base costs change per provider. The same Bella+Canvas 3001 t-shirt costs about $4.45 on Printify and $8.95 on Printful - a 100% difference on the single biggest line item of a merch order. If you build your price on one provider's number and the order routes to another provider, your margin evaporates before you notice.

Leak #3 is presentation. Quotes that look unprofessional get negotiated down. When a client sees a bare price list, they push back; when they see the product on a model or in a realistic mockup, they accept the number. Presentation is part of pricing - and it is the part AI tools help with the most, because the marginal cost of a good mockup is now close to zero.
The 5-Step AI-Assisted Pricing Workflow
Step 1 - Make the file print-ready before you price it (Claid AI)

Every quote starts with a file audit. I check resolution, color space (RGB vs CMYK), and bleed. If a supplier or customer file is below 300 DPI at the target print size, I upscale it with Claid AI before I price the job. Claid's free tier caps exports at 96 DPI, which is not print-ready, so real print work needs the Pro plan - around $49/month for roughly 500 renders, which covers about 2,000 products a year for a small shop. The economics are simple: one avoided reprint pays for a week of the plan. Claid also sharpens edges and cleans noise, which improves the printed result, not just the file spec. This is the layer that protects your margin before you ever write a number.
Step 2 - Know your design cost (Kittl, Creative Fabrica)

If you design your own merch, your design tool is a fixed cost that belongs in every price you quote. Kittl's Pro plan at $15/month (about $10-12/mo annual) with SVG export replaces a $30-60/month vector suite for most POD work, and SVG output keeps edges crisp at any print size - which removes another reprint risk from the chain. If you buy ready-made designs instead, Creative Fabrica's Craft Club at $4.99/month covers licensed assets, and the license check belongs in your pricing checklist: an unlicensed design can cost you the entire run, not just the margin.
Step 3 - Run the real cost math (Printify, Printful, Gelato calculators)

Platform calculators do the arithmetic, but you have to feed them the right numbers. I price the same product on at least two platforms before I commit: base cost, print price per color, shipping to my top three destinations, and any per-order fees. Gelato's local-production model matters if you sell into the EU - 140+ hubs in 32 countries mean a German customer's shirt ships from a German hub, which changes both the shipping line and the customs exposure on your quote. Printful's 340+ product catalog is smaller but in-house, while Printify's 850+ product network is a marketplace of competing print providers - the price difference between providers on the same product is often larger than the difference between platforms. Both platforms publish their numbers openly, which makes the math repeatable: Printify's pricing pages, Printful's pricing pages, and Gelato's pricing page are the tabs I keep open while quoting.
Step 4 - Build margin with a formula, not a guess

My formula after the test: price = (base cost + shipping + per-order fees) divided by (1 - platform cut - 0.05 buffer). On a $4.45 Printify shirt with $3.95 shipping and Etsy's 6.5% plus $0.25, a $24.99 price leaves about $8.90 gross margin - roughly 36%. The same shirt priced at $19.99 leaves about $4.30. At ten sales a day, that is the difference between $89 and $43 a day; over a month, it is a $1,380 swing on the exact same product. The formula does not replace judgment - it makes the judgment visible, which is what lets you defend a price to a client or raise it without guilt.
Step 5 - Present the quote like a pro (Mockey mockups)

Before I send a quote or launch a listing, I put the design on the actual product with Mockey. At $9.99/month with batch generation, I can show a client three colorways on a hoodie in ten minutes instead of ordering samples and waiting a week. In my test, mockup presentation was the single fastest win: quotes that included a realistic mockup closed at full price, while bare price lists got negotiated down. For print-shop clients, a mockup of their packaging or branded merch turns a commodity quote into a design conversation - and design conversations do not get shopped around.
The 4 Pricing Mistakes I See Print Sellers Make

items: Pricing from one platform's base cost and never re-checking. Base costs shift quarterly and differ per provider - on Printify, the same product can vary by 15-30% between print providers in the network.
Ignoring the file until it fails. A file that needs a reprint is a file that was mispriced twice: once in the quote, once on press. The file audit in Step 1 costs five minutes.

Rolling all fees into one mental number. Etsy fees, payment processing, and shipping each move independently. When one of them rises, sellers who blended them into a single guess absorb the rise in margin instead of the price.
Sending quotes without visuals. Every negotiated-down quote in my history was a text-only price list. Every mockup-backed quote held its number.

What MagicDrop Was (and Why Beginners Loved It)

MagicDrop launched around 2021-2022 as a print-on-demand platform built on AliExpress sourcing. The pitch was simple and genuinely appealing to new sellers: pick a product from a huge AliExpress catalog (hats, tote bags, phone cases, cushions, home decor), upload your design, and MagicDrop would source the blank, print it, and ship it after each sale. No inventory, no minimum order quantity, no monthly fee for the basic workflow.

The cost advantage was the hook. AliExpress blanks are dramatically cheaper than US-based blank suppliers, so the per-unit cost on products like embroidered caps or poly tote bags was often the lowest of any POD model I tracked. For a beginner on Etsy or Shopify who wanted to test dozens of designs without committing money to inventory, that combination was objectively attractive. It was one of several 'AliExpress POD' platforms - MagicDrop, AliDrop, and similar services - that rode the 2021-2023 POD boom.

But the same structural choice that created the low prices also created the trust problem. Because the platform did not own the printing, the blanks, or the logistics, every order depended on a chain of third-party suppliers. When that chain works, you get a cheap product. When it does not, you get a confused customer and a support ticket that takes days to resolve.

The operational flow also created a hidden cost that beginners rarely counted: because every order was a cross-border transaction, tracking updates were patchy and customs delays were common. A seller could not simply promise 'ships in 3 days' the way a Printful or Printify store can. Pricing had to bake in a long tail of support time - answering 'where is my order' messages, chasing suppliers, and re-sending replacements - which quietly ate the margin advantage the cheap blanks had created in the first place.

items: Shipping times. Because products came from AliExpress suppliers, door-to-door delivery to US and EU customers often took 2-4 weeks. items: Domain and status. Does the platform's own site serve real product pages, a pricing page, and a support page? A site that only redirects or shows a parking lander is the number one red flag in 2026.
Order of operations. Can you place a test order today, or is there a waiting list, an invite wall, or a 'contact us' gate?
Ownership of the print. Does the company own its fulfillment, or does it resell a network of third parties? Ownership is not required - but you must know who is accountable when a print is bad.

Shipping promises. What is the actual door-to-door time to your main market? Cheap AliExpress-sourced POD is cheap partly because shipping is slow - price that into your margin math before you advertise fast delivery.
Refund policy in writing. Find the refund and replacement clause before you sell, not after the first customer complaint.
Review quality, not volume. Check Trustpilot and Shopify App Store reviews for recurring patterns (QC, shipping, payouts), not just star counts. Five stars from three reviews tells you nothing.
A paper trail. An active blog, changelog, or support documentation updated this year is a good sign. A site whose news section stopped in 2023 is a warning.

If you came here asking 'is MagicDrop legit' because you saw a YouTube video or an old blog post that still recommends it: do not sign up for anything on magicdrop.com, because there is nothing to sign up for. Treat the platform as inactive and move on. The practical plan for 2026 looks like this:

blocks.text: One more honest note before you go: I have no financial or personal stake in MagicDrop's story either way, and I am not calling the founders scammers - the documented failure mode here is operational, not criminal. blocks.text: Licensing in Plain Language (the Part Most Sellers Skip)

The single most common way a free-asset haul turns into a problem is the license question, so let me be concrete. Creative Fabrica's standard license for free picks generally allows commercial use of the asset in physical products - a t-shirt you print and sell is a physical product, and that is the core POD use case. What the standard license typically does not grant without extra terms is mass reproduction for resale (printing the asset itself on bulk products and selling the product as a generic item, rather than a designed product), and some bundles carry Extended Licenses that are required for certain digital resale or large-scale runs. The practical rule I use: one designed product with the asset as a component is fine; a product that is essentially the raw asset with nothing added is risky. If the listing page shows a license tab, open it; if it mentions POD or Print on Demand explicitly, read that clause twice. title: Printful and Printify Merger (FYUL): What POD Sellers Need to Know in 2026
metaDescription: Printful and Printify merged under FYUL in November 2024. What actually changed for your store and pricing - explained with real numbers and what to watch in 2026.
tldr: Printful and Printify merged in November 2024 and now sit under one parent company, FYUL - but both platforms still operate independently with separate accounts, catalogs, and support.
The visible changes so far: Printify Premium rose from $29 to $39/month (monthly billing) and Printful adjusted selected shipping rates - moves analysts link to a possible FYUL IPO in 2026-2027.
For sellers: no forced migration and no merged catalog. The Printful vs Printify choice is still real - keep both options open and re-check pricing every quarter.

blocks.text: I have run a print-on-demand store since 2021, so when Printful and Printify - the two platforms my store, and most POD stores, are built on - announced in November 2024 that they were merging into one company, I paid close attention. By January 2025 the combined group had a new name: FYUL, a parent brand that also houses Snow Commerce. Since then I have tracked every pricing change, every announcement, and every migration rumor from a seller's perspective. This is what I have learned: what the merger actually changed for sellers, what stayed exactly the same, and what to watch through the rest of 2026.
See our roundup of the best Printful alternatives and the best Printify alternatives if you want more options side by side.
The Short Version: What Happened

In November 2024, Printful and Printify announced they would merge under a new parent company. Regulatory approvals and shareholder backing followed, and in January 2025 the combined group launched under the name FYUL, which also includes Snow Commerce, a Shopify-focused commerce company. The merger created by far the largest company in print-on-demand: between them, Printful and Printify already fulfilled a majority of independent POD orders worldwide, and running them under one roof changed the economics of the whole industry.

rows: No immediate changes; both platforms kept operating as before
New parent name; seller accounts and dashboards untouched
First visible pricing move under the shared parent
Selected US and EU shipping rates revised
Analysts expect more cost discipline and possible price harmonization

blocks.text: Why the Merger Happened (and Why It Matters for Your Margins)

Two platform companies with overlapping markets rarely merge to save money on servers; they merge to control the market. Printful and Printify spent years competing on price, catalog size, and print quality - a rivalry that kept base costs low and forced both to keep improving. Under FYUL, that competition happens inside one company. Industry coverage in 2026 consistently frames the merger as preparation for a possible IPO in 2026 or 2027, and an IPO-grade company manages margins, not rivalries. For sellers the direct consequence is simple: expect pricing decisions that protect the combined business, not discounts that win a turf war.
Does the Merger Change My Printify or Printful Account?

No - and this is the most important thing to understand, because most of the scary headlines assume otherwise. Both platforms continue to operate as separate apps. You keep the same Printful account and the same Printify account, each with its own dashboard, product catalog, billing, and support channel. Your listings, integrations, and provider choices do not change. There is no merged catalog, no forced account migration, and no single sign-on. As of August 2026, the only sign of the shared parent you will notice in day-to-day work is occasional FYUL-branded announcement emails.

items: Your Printful and Printify accounts, dashboards, and order history remain separate and unchanged.
Product catalogs: Printify still lists 1,300+ products across 85+ independent providers; Printful still offers its curated 300+ in-house catalog.
Billing and plans: the free tiers, Printful Growth, and Printify Premium are still billed separately per platform.
Integrations: Shopify, Etsy, Amazon, WooCommerce, TikTok Shop, and the rest keep working exactly as before.
Support: each platform has its own help center, chat, and account team - there is no merged support queue.

blocks.text: What HAS Changed for Sellers So Far

The changes under FYUL have been gradual and mostly behind the scenes - cost discipline, consolidated operations, and preparation for a possible IPO. But two changes have been visible to sellers, and both move the margin math I recalculate every quarter:

rows: Monthly price rose from $29 to $39 (annual stays $24.99/mo billed yearly)
Break-even moves to roughly 15-17 orders/month; annual plan now saves about 36% vs monthly
Selected US and EU rates revised in 2026 H1
Re-check your top products; shipping changes hit margin harder than base cost
Both catalogs remain separate as of mid-2026
No single merged product list; likely revisited after an IPO
Some FYUL-branded emails from both brands

blocks.text: FYUL 2026 Capacity Bet: The Riga Move Sellers Should Watch

The most concrete post-merger investment is physical, not digital. In December 2025 FYUL confirmed it is relocating its team to a new 97,000-square-foot facility in Riga, Latvia, with the move expected to finish in the first quarter of 2026 (ASI Central). That is roughly triple the 30,138 sq ft Riga fulfillment center Printful opened in 2020 (Printful newsroom), and it is the clearest signal yet that the merged company is consolidating European operations into one large footprint.

The same announcement cycle revealed FYUL House: a state-of-the-art 9,000 sqm dual-building headquarters in Riga that the combined Printful, Printify, and Snow Commerce teams had already begun moving into by late November 2025 (Labs of Latvia). For sellers, the signal is capacity: after years of running separate networks, the combined company is concentrating its European fulfillment planning in one large, modern site.

What this means for your delivery promises: (1) EU fulfillment is where Printful historically held its strongest in-house advantage, and the Riga expansion protects European production times as cross-border volume grows; (2) a single larger facility typically means more automated capacity, which usually shows up as steadier production estimates during Q4 peaks; and (3) the rebrand - Printful, Printify, and Snow Commerce now all sit under the FYUL name (Labs of Latvia) - means the platforms will keep sharing infrastructure even while their storefront apps stay separate.

items: Re-verify EU shipping rates on your top five products: the Riga consolidation can change regional rate tables even when base prices do not move.
Watch Q4 production estimates in October: a newly consolidated facility usually stabilizes lead times, but the first peak season after a move is the one to monitor.
Keep both apps installed: the facility move is infrastructure, not a product change - Printful and Printify storefronts remain independent as of August 2026.
If you sell to EU buyers, prefer the platform whose EU hub matches your biggest market; Riga serves the Baltic-Nordic and Northern EU corridor fastest.

blocks.text: The seller checklist in practice: none of this requires you to change accounts, catalogs, or integrations. It changes the context you should watch. A larger European footprint lowers the odds of capacity-driven delays and raises the odds of steadier pricing from a combined network - both are mild positives for POD sellers who ship to Europe, and neutral for sellers focused on the US market.
Printify Premium Price Rise: The Break-Even Math

The clearest post-merger signal is Printify Premium's monthly price rising from $29 to $39 in early 2026. The annual plan stayed at $24.99 per month billed yearly, which quietly changed the value equation: before the increase, annual billing saved about 14 percent versus monthly; after it, annual billing saves about 36 percent. That is a textbook pre-IPO retention nudge - lock sellers into yearly commitments. For a store doing 10 to 15 orders a month, Premium's up-to-20-percent product discount previously paid for itself around the 12-order mark; at the new monthly price the break-even moves to roughly 15 to 17 orders. If you are under that volume, the free plan or the annual plan is now clearly the rational choice.
Printful Shipping Adjustments in 2026

Printful's visible change has been shipping, not subscription pricing. During the first half of 2026 the company revised selected US and EU shipping rates as part of the group-wide cost review. Shipping is where margin quietly disappears, so this matters more than it looks: a $1.50 increase on a $6 shipping charge is a 25 percent cost swing on that line item, and it hits every order, not just premium ones. If you sell on Printful, re-check shipping on your top five products this month rather than assuming last year's rates still apply.
Snow Commerce: The Part Most Sellers Miss

FYUL is not just Printful plus Printify; it also includes Snow Commerce, which builds and operates Shopify stores for large brands. That gives the group an enterprise arm selling to big merchants - and it explains why FYUL's roadmap emphasizes Shopify integrations and AI-assisted design tools. For independent sellers the practical effect is neutral-to-positive: features that large clients demand, like better APIs, faster mockups, and bulk tools, tend to trickle down to everyone.
Should You Still Compare Printful vs Printify?

Yes - and here is why. A shared parent company does not make two platforms the same product. Printify is still a marketplace that routes your orders to independent print providers for the lowest base costs and the largest catalog. Printful is still a vertically integrated printer with in-house production, the most consistent quality, and the strongest branding options. My full side-by-side comparison still applies, and the quick version looks like this:
What the Merger Means for the Wider POD Market
The merger changes the competitive map of print-on-demand in three ways that matter even if you never touch Printful or Printify again:

items: Less price competition between the two giants: the rivalry that kept base costs sharp now happens under one roof. Expect coordinated pricing, not discount wars.
More pressure on independent print providers: Printify's provider network is central to the group's value, so expect stricter vetting and, over time, fewer but better providers.
Stronger challengers: Gelato, Gooten, Prodigi, and regional players now market directly against the merged giant - often with better deals and faster features for sellers who shop around.

blocks.text: Should New Sellers Still Start with Printful or Printify?

Yes - the merger does not change the on-ramp. Both platforms still offer genuinely free plans with no monthly fee and no credit card, which makes them the easiest way for a new Etsy or Shopify seller to start testing designs today. What I tell new sellers is slightly different post-merger: start on one platform, but keep a second option warm. The free tier costs you nothing, so opening a Printful account even if you print on Printify gives you a tested fallback if pricing shifts after an IPO. And do not ignore the challengers - Gelato's local-production model and Prodigi's enterprise tools are both worth a sample order before you commit a whole catalog.
Etsy vs Shopify Sellers: Does the Merger Change Your Stack?

For Etsy sellers the merger changes little operationally: both platforms integrate with Etsy the same way they did before, and Etsy orders flow to whichever platform you connected. For Shopify sellers, the enterprise angle is more visible - Snow Commerce's Shopify expertise is being folded into the group's roadmap, so expect richer Shopify integrations and AI-assisted mockup features to arrive first on the combined platform. What I have not seen yet is any difference in how the two brands treat Etsy sellers versus Shopify sellers; plan selection and pricing are identical regardless of channel.
What I Did After the Merger: Sample Orders and Quarterly Re-checks

What the merger changed is my maintenance routine. I now re-check base costs and shipping on both platforms every quarter, because FYUL-era pricing drifts quietly. That quarterly check takes me about 45 minutes and has already caught two shipping changes that would have shaved my margin.
My Bottom Line After 20 Months of Watching the Merger

My honest conclusion is anticlimactic: nothing dramatic has happened, and that is exactly the point. The merger's biggest impact so far is pricing drift - Printify Premium up, Printful shipping adjusted - not platform disruption. Sellers who panic-consolidated to one platform in early 2025 gained nothing, because the platforms stayed separate. Keep both platforms, use each for what it is best at, and keep your business portable: with an IPO on the table, having a tested alternative to the merged group is cheap insurance.

The habit is a quarterly pricing review: base cost, shipping, and plan tier on both platforms, about 45 minutes. Quick Verdict: Printify for Margins, Printful for Consistency

If you are a margin-hungry Halloween seller testing lots of designs, start on Printify: base costs run roughly $4 lower per unit on comparable apparel, the catalog is 3x bigger, and provider competition keeps prices competitive. If you are building a cohesive Halloween brand — matching sublimation mugs, blankets, and ornaments where color accuracy and print placement must be identical every single order — Printful's in-house production is worth the premium.
Why Halloween Is POD's Biggest Seasonal Window

Every POD seller knows the Q4 calendar, but Halloween is the window where a tiny store can actually outrun the big brands: shoppers search for specific, funny, niche designs ("Halloween dad shirt", "spooky cat mom", "goth Christmas"), and those long-tail queries have almost no competition until mid-September. Etsy keyword data I tracked last year shows Halloween searches starting their climb around August 15 and compounding weekly until the first week of October. That means every day of the next month is a compounding traffic day — which is exactly why the catalog and margin decisions below matter now, not in October.

items: Mid-August: search volume starts rising — the moment to have your first 10-20 listings live so Etsy's algorithm has time to index them.
September 1-15: first orders arrive; you learn which designs convert before peak CPC inflation.
October 1: last practical date for US orders to arrive before Halloween parties (5-9 day shipping means mid-September is the real production deadline).
October 15-31: the rush — your listings are proven, rankings are sticky, and margin per order is at its seasonal best.

blocks.text: Halloween Catalogs: What Each Platform Actually Carries

This is where the two platforms diverge most. Printful runs an in-house catalog of roughly 340 products, with a dedicated Halloween collection page that bundles seasonal apparel, mugs, and home goods. Printify is a network of 100+ independent print providers offering more than 1,000 products (their own count is 1,300+), with a bestseller catalog that rotates by season. For Halloween specifically, both carry the essentials — tees, hoodies, mugs, tote bags — but the long tail is very different.

items: A curated Halloween collection page — seasonal designs and product bundles maintained by Printful's own team, which is useful for niche research.

You do not need a designer budget for Halloween — the free-asset approach covers most of these, and both platforms handle them well. Quick Answer: Is GearLaunch Legit in 2026?

GearLaunch is a real, operating business - not a scam. What the Trustpilot Data Shows (Verified 19 Aug 2026)

What matters is the pattern: a non-accredited profile plus a 1.71/5 average plus a 2.5/5 Trustpilot score triangulate to the same story.
Is GearLaunch a Scam? No - But the Complaint Patterns Matter

No, GearLaunch is not a scam. It is a print-on-demand company with real fulfillment operations in the US and EU, a public product catalog, and an active Shopify integration. My hands-on review of the platform is here: GearLaunch Review 2026. What the review data does show is a recurring theme: the gap between marketing and fulfillment experience. Across the Trustpilot and BBB record, the recurring complaints center on print quality consistency, refund handling, and slower-than-promised production around peak seasons. I am not repeating any single anecdote as fact here - but a pattern repeated across hundreds of reviews is data, and you should price it into your decision.

The "not a scam" framing matters for one practical reason: unlike the MagicDrop case we documented earlier (a platform whose domain ended up parked and for sale), GearLaunch is still operating and fulfilling orders today. The risk is not that it disappears with your money - the risk is that your store's reputation rides on fulfillment quality that public reviewers rate poorly.
